text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Tension emerges between Bonn and Ankara over a planned visit to Turkey by German members of parliament.
- Liberal Free Democrats (FDP) may be ready to accept a delay in cutting the solidarity surcharge on income tax to prevent a rise in petroleum tax.
- Federal Accounting Office says government must improve planning and checking of subsidies it distributes.
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem urges caution in debate over reform of penions system.
- Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing says countries should not use budgetary tricks to meet Maastricht criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
HANDELSBLATT
- Head of Federal Accounting Office accuses public sector of not knowing how to deal with tight budgets.
- Bundesbank calls for subsidies to eastern Germany to be gradually reduced.
- Education Minister Juergen Ruettgers says 100,000 new traineeships and apprenticeships needed by year 2005.
- President Roman Herzog calls for even closer contact between Germany and France.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Coalition considering delay in cut in solidarity surcharge as opposition mounts to raising petroleum tax.
- Coalition parties reject proposal by opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to bring forward planned tax reform by one year to 1998.
- Deutsche Telekom to announce on Monday price range for shares in its forthcoming flotation.
DIE WELT
- Christian Democrats (CDU) demand early elections in state of Saxony-Anhalt, where SPD and Greens rule with tolerance of former communist PDS.
- Private households falling increasingly into debt, Bundesbank monthly report shows.
- Berlin regional government fails to agree on savings measures.
- Germany will be "considerably" over its budget deficit target of 60 billion marks this year, Bundesbank says.
